newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian troops ready for PNG, some expats leave.
newsitem.headline: Australian troops ready for PNG, some expats leave.

text.p: Australian Foreign Affairs Minister Alexander Downer said on Sunday that Australian defence forces had been upgraded to a higher degree of readiness as a result of the political crisis in Papua New Guinea (PNG).
However, he again declined to comment on whether Australia had plans to send troops to PNG as a peacekeeping force.

Downer made the comments as The Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd (BHP, Australia's biggest company, said it had closed its Port Moresby steel processing plant and had begun to evacuate dependants following street violence last week.

"We can't go into the details of private discussions that many of us have been having with senior officials and political figures in Papua New Guinea," Downer said in a television interview when asked if Australian forces would be sent to PNG.

"I can really only say in relation to the Australian defence force that there has been some upgrading of its level of readiness, but that is of course just a natural precaution, an understandable precaution, for the Australian government to take," Downer said.

Newspapers have reported that the PNG government had formally requested that Australia send troops to PNG after self-proclaimed army leader Major Walter Enuma on Saturday again ordered Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan to resign by Tuesday.
Enuma said the defence forces remained loyal to sacked army commander Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok and threatened confrontation if any attempts were made to disarm them.
About 10,000 Australians live in PNG, which was administered by Australia until 1975, and Australia is PNG's biggest foreign investor with investments of more than US$3 billion.
Australia is also PNG's biggest aid donor, contributing about $260 million a year, including about $10 million in military aid.
BHP chief executive John Prescott said in a television interview that BHP closed its Port Moresby plant last week and had evacuated or would evacuate all expatriates and dependants.
He said BHP operations in other parts of PNG, including the big Ok Tedi copper/gold mine, were running normally.
Prescott said 10 to 15 employees and dependants have been or would be flown out of Port Moresby. "If you're talking about non-nationals, we're not likely to have anyone in Port Moresby."
A spokesman for Qantas Airways said flights to Australia were booked more fully than normal on both Qantas and Air Niugini, but there were no signs of a mass exodus of expatriates.
Downer said it was his impression that General Singirok had the significant support of the Papua New Guinea defence force.
"(But) we have no reason to believe at this stage that General Singirok is taking a view that the constitution shouldn't be kept in place and upheld," he added.
Downer said it appeared some calm had returned to the capital of Port Moresby after two days of street violence last week, but that the level of background tension remained high.
The crisis began last Monday when Singirok demanded Chan quit over his hiring of 70 foreign mercenaries to help quell the nine-year secessionist rebellion on Bougainville Island.
Singirok was promptly fired and replaced by Colonel Alfred Aikung. Singirok's supporters, led by Enuma, have demanded that the former commander be given back his job.
The Australian government has advised Australians to stay away from Papua New Guinea unless travel is essential.
